threads.thread_goal: Align on target segments and top cross-sell opportunities for Q3.

messages.text: Kicking off the Q3 cross-sell work here. For this first step we need to lock our target customer segments and the top cross-sell opportunities per segment so we can progress T1 and T4 and start filling A1. My proposal is to focus on three segment lenses: 1) existing mid-market customers with only a single product, 2) enterprise accounts with renewal in Q3, and 3) high-growth SMBs in year 1. For each, we should shortlist three product pairings that are realistic for Q3. @231 @468837 can you react to this segmentation and suggest the top three pairings per segment based on what you see in the field

Thanks for framing this. The three lenses make sense, but I would like to clarify definitions so we do not mix segments later in A1. For mid-market, are we using the same revenue band as in our current territory plan And for high-growth SMBs, do we define them by year-on-year revenue growth or by product usage expansion Once we agree on that, I can propose three pairings per segment and document the assumptions for T1.

Good call on definitions. Suggesting: mid-market as 1 to 10 million annual revenue, aligned with the current territory model; enterprise as above 10 million; SMB as below 1 million. For high-growth SMBs, let us use at least 30 percent year-on-year revenue growth or a 50 percent increase in active users over the last 6 months, whichever is available. If that works for you, can you and @468837 each propose your top three pairings per segment so we can compare and converge into A1

I am aligned with those definitions. From a field perspective, for mid-market single product customers, the most natural pairings I see are: 1) core platform plus analytics add-on, 2) core platform plus premium support, 3) analytics add-on plus training package. For enterprise renewals, I would go with: 1) analytics add-on plus governance module, 2) premium support plus training package, 3) governance module plus integration services. For high-growth SMBs, I would suggest: 1) starter package plus analytics light, 2) starter package plus onboarding support, 3) analytics light plus email automation. Happy to adjust once @231 shares their view so we can finalize T4.

I agree with the segment definitions. Looking at recent deals, my proposal is close to what @468837 suggested, with a few tweaks. Mid-market: 1) core platform plus analytics add-on, 2) core platform plus integration services, 3) analytics add-on plus training package. Enterprise renewals: 1) analytics add-on plus governance module, 2) governance module plus integration services, 3) premium support plus training package. High-growth SMBs: 1) starter package plus onboarding support, 2) starter package plus analytics light, 3) analytics light plus email automation. I can start drafting these into A1 with estimated uplift ranges for T1 and T4 if we agree on this direction.

Jumping in to check one thing before we lock this. For the enterprise segment, do we want to differentiate between accounts with global contracts versus regional ones The governance module plus integration services pairing might be more realistic for global accounts where we already have central sponsorship. If we agree, we could note that nuance in A1 so reps know where to prioritize.

Good point. I suggest we keep the three enterprise pairings as proposed by @231 but add a note in A1 that governance plus integration is primarily for global contracts, while analytics plus governance is suitable for both global and regional. That way we do not overcomplicate the matrix but still guide prioritization. If there are no objections, @231 can proceed to draft A1 with that nuance.

Quick question on the SMB definition. For accounts where we do not have reliable revenue data but we see strong product usage, should we still treat them as high-growth SMBs for this playbook Or do we keep them out of scope for now I want to make sure we do not confuse reps when they look at A1.

If we lack revenue data but see a 50 percent or higher increase in active users over 6 months, we will treat them as high-growth SMBs for the purpose of this playbook. I will ask our data team offline to flag those accounts in the CRM, but for now we can document this rule in A1 so it is explicit for T1 completion.

Understood. I will take the segment definitions and the agreed pairings and start populating A1. I will include: 1) the three segments with the revenue and growth criteria, 2) the three product pairings per segment, 3) a short note on when to prioritize governance plus integration for global enterprise accounts, and 4) initial uplift ranges based on last year data. I will share a draft for review before we call T1 and T4 done.

Once A1 draft is ready, I can sanity check the uplift assumptions against my region pipeline and add comments where the ranges feel too optimistic or conservative. That should help us avoid unrealistic expectations later when we set targets.

I have uploaded the first draft of A1 with the three segments and the three pairings per segment, including the notes we discussed. Uplift ranges are based on last year cross-sell conversion rates by segment. Please review and comment, especially on the SMB uplift where data is thinner. After your feedback, I suggest we freeze the segment list and pairings so we can move on to the playbook content.

I reviewed A1 and left comments on two SMB pairings where the uplift looked slightly high compared to the last quarter. Apart from that, the structure and segment definitions look consistent with our current territory model. From my side, I am comfortable using this as the base for the rest of the project.

I also went through A1 and added a couple of notes on enterprise uplift, but overall the three segments and the three pairings per segment match what we see in the field. I do not have any blocking concerns. Once we adjust the two SMB ranges that @173966 flagged, I think we can close T1 and T4 from a sales perspective.

I have updated the SMB uplift ranges in A1 based on the comments from @173966 and @468837. The rest of the matrix remains unchanged. Unless there are new objections today, I suggest we treat this as our final segment list and top three cross-sell opportunities per segment for Q3.

Thanks all for the iterations on A1. To summarize where we landed for the Q3 cross-sell playbook: 1) we will focus on three segments, mid-market single product customers, enterprise accounts with Q3 renewals, and high-growth SMBs as defined in the matrix; 2) for each segment we have three agreed product pairings documented in A1 with uplift ranges and notes on when to prioritize each. With that, I am marking the segment list as approved and the top three cross-sell opportunities per segment as selected so we can move forward with the playbook drafting.
Noted on the final segments and pairings. I will use A1 as the reference when we later review the training and communication pieces so that examples stay consistent with what was approved here.
Next step from here is for the project team to use A1 as the backbone for the playbook structure in T2 and the opportunity mapping in the dashboard spec for T5. I will start that in the next thread.

threads.thread_goal: Review and finalize the first version of the cross-sell playbook.

messages.text: As a follow up to the segment and pairing decisions in A1, I have drafted Cross-Sell Sales Playbook v1 in A2 and a first pass of the KPI and dashboard spec in A3. A2 covers stages, steps, responsibilities, and messaging for each segment, and I mapped the main steps to existing CRM fields as part of T2 and T3. A3 outlines the KPIs we will track for T5. Please review A2 and A3 and share feedback on structure, clarity for reps, and any CRM alignment gaps you see.

I went through A2 and overall the flow is logical. One concern is that the discovery stage has five separate qualification questions plus two optional ones. Given the time reps have with customers, I would suggest we reduce this to three core questions and keep the rest as prompts in the notes. Also, in the mid-market path, the step about logging cross-sell intent in the CRM references a field that some teams do not use consistently. We should confirm with the CRM admin whether that field is mandatory or if we should rely on an existing stage or tag instead for T3.

On A3, I like the focus on a small set of KPIs. I have a question on the proposed cross-sell pipeline coverage metric. You defined it as cross-sell pipeline value divided by total pipeline value. For Q3, do we want to track that by segment as well or only at the aggregate level If we can break it down by segment without extra CRM fields, that might help us see where the playbook is working best.

I had a quick look at A2 and I am not fully sure how the enterprise renewal path differs from the mid-market one in terms of approvals. The steps look similar. Should we add a note that enterprise deals must follow the existing discount governance in A4, or is that assumed I want to avoid confusion for reps who are new to these accounts.

Agree on simplifying the discovery stage. I will reduce it to three mandatory qualification questions and move the rest into a guidance section so we keep the playbook lean. On the CRM field, I already checked with the admin when working on T3. The cross-sell intent field is optional today and not consistently used, so in A2 I proposed using the existing opportunity type plus a cross-sell tag instead. I will make that clearer in the text and in the mapping table so there is no ambiguity.

For the cross-sell pipeline coverage metric in A3, we can break it down by segment using the existing segment field in the CRM, so no new fields are needed. I will update A3 to show the metric both at total level and by the three segments from A1. That should help us later when we do the post-launch review and T12.

Good catch. The enterprise renewal path should explicitly reference the existing discount and approval governance in A4. I will add a step in A2 that reminds reps to follow the standard approval thresholds and exceptions process, and I will link to A4 in the playbook. That way we stay aligned with T10 even though that task is more focused on documenting governance.

From a field usability angle, I like that A2 is structured by segment. One suggestion: in the high-growth SMB path, could we add a simple checklist at the end of the call prep section, similar to what we plan for A6 later That would help newer reps remember to confirm product fit, timing, and budget without reading long paragraphs. Also, in A3, the win rate metric might need a minimum number of opportunities per segment to avoid noisy percentages in smaller territories.

I agree on the minimum volume for the win rate metric. Maybe we can define in A3 that we only show segment level win rate if there are at least 10 cross-sell opportunities in that segment for the period. Below that, we could show counts only. That should keep the dashboard from being misleading.

Good suggestions. I will add a short three point checklist to the high-growth SMB path in A2, aligned with what we will later include in A6, and I will update A3 so that segment level win rate is only displayed when there are at least 10 cross-sell opportunities in that segment for the selected period. Otherwise we will show counts and hide the percentage.

Thanks for clarifying the CRM field mapping. With the simplified discovery questions and the explicit reference to the cross-sell tag, I think the playbook will be easier to adopt. One last detail: in the mid-market path, can we add a reminder to log the secondary product interest as a separate line item when relevant That will help us later when we analyze product level performance in A3.

Yes, I will add a short reminder in the mid-market path to log the secondary product as a separate line item when appropriate, and I will reflect that in the data mapping section of A3 so the dashboard can break down performance by primary and secondary products without new fields.

I rechecked the enterprise path in A2 after your edits and the reference to A4 is now clear. The steps also match the current approval thresholds we use in other playbooks, so I do not see any misalignment with existing workflows.

With the segment breakdown added in A3 and the minimum volume rule for win rate, the KPI set looks balanced. We have volume, value, and conversion metrics without overloading the dashboard. From my side, T5 can move forward once finance validates the targets later.

I have now incorporated all the feedback into A2 and A3: simplified discovery, clear CRM field mapping using existing fields, explicit reference to A4 for enterprise approvals, segment level KPIs with minimum volume rules, and the SMB checklist. I also revalidated the CRM alignment with the admin for T3 and they confirmed we are not introducing any new mandatory fields. Unless there are new comments today, I propose we treat this as the final structure and key steps for the playbook and confirm that it is aligned with current CRM workflows.

I am comfortable with A2 and A3 as they stand. The stages, steps, and responsibilities are clear, and the CRM mapping reflects how reps work today. From a sales side, I support closing this version so we can move on to the pilot design.
Same here. The updated A2 feels usable in real conversations, and the CRM alignment looks practical. I do not see any blockers from the field perspective.

Thanks for the reviews. Summarizing: 1) we are aligned on the playbook structure in A2, including stages, steps, responsibilities, and simplified discovery; 2) A2 now clearly references A4 for enterprise approvals; 3) A3 defines a focused KPI set with segment breakdowns and minimum volume rules; and 4) CRM admin has confirmed that the mapping in T3 uses existing fields and workflows without adding new mandatory fields. Based on this, I am marking the playbook structure and key steps as agreed and confirming that the playbook is aligned with current CRM workflows so we can proceed to pilot planning.

threads.thread_goal: Define pilot scope, participants, and success criteria.

messages.text: Starting the pilot planning here. Building on A2 and A3, I drafted a pilot outline for T6: scope is 4 weeks, focusing on mid-market and high-growth SMB segments only, using the new playbook steps in A2 and tracking KPIs from A3. Proposal is to run the pilot with one mid-market team and one SMB team, around 8 to 10 reps total. Success would be measured by cross-sell opportunity creation rate, win rate, and qualitative feedback that we will later summarize in A5 for T7. Looking for input on which teams to involve and whether 4 weeks feels right.

From a coverage standpoint, 4 weeks should be enough to see early signals, especially in mid-market. For teams, I suggest we use the central mid-market pod that already has some cross-sell experience and the SMB pod that handles high-growth accounts in the north region. They are used to testing new approaches and usually give structured feedback, which will help with A5. One question: are we excluding enterprise entirely from the pilot, or do we want at least one enterprise rep to try the renewal path from A2

I like the idea of focusing on mid-market and SMB first. For success metrics, in addition to opportunity creation and win rate, could we track the percentage of eligible calls where reps actually used the playbook steps That would give us an adoption signal, not just outcomes. We might be able to approximate that by checking how often the cross-sell tag and the new checklist fields are filled in the CRM, as defined in A3.

I have a small concern about the 8 to 10 reps target. If one or two are on vacation or pulled into another initiative, we might end up with very few active users. Should we aim for 10 to 12 reps instead, so we have some buffer Even if a couple of them only partially adopt the playbook, we would still have enough data for A5.

On including enterprise, my suggestion is to keep the main pilot focused on mid-market and high-growth SMB, but invite 2 enterprise reps who have Q3 renewals coming up to use the renewal path from A2 on a best effort basis. We can capture their feedback separately in A5 without making enterprise metrics a core success criterion for this first pilot.

Good point on adoption. We can add a pilot metric in A3 for percentage of eligible opportunities where the cross-sell tag and checklist fields are filled. For the pilot, we will track that for the selected teams only. I will update the pilot section of A3 accordingly and make sure T6 reflects this as a success criterion.

Agree on the risk of low active users. Let us target 12 reps total: 6 in the mid-market pod, 4 in the SMB pod, plus 2 enterprise reps as suggested by @137952. That should give us enough volume even with some absence. I will reflect that in the T6 pilot scope.

For the mid-market pod, I can confirm 6 reps who are comfortable with cross-sell conversations and have bandwidth in the next month. I will align with their manager and share the final list of names so you can include it in the T6 document. For the enterprise reps, I suggest we ask their manager to nominate two people who already own Q3 renewals.

On the SMB side, I can secure 4 reps from the high-growth pod in the north region. They have a good volume of opportunities and are used to testing new scripts. I will confirm their names and expected start date so we can lock the pilot timeline.

For feedback collection, how do we want reps to share their qualitative input during the pilot Should we set up a short weekly survey plus one group call at the end, or rely only on interviews I want to make sure we do not overload them but still get enough detail for A5 and T7.

I propose a light structure: 1) a 5 minute weekly pulse survey with 3 questions on clarity, usability, and customer reaction; 2) one 45 minute group call at the end of the 4 weeks with all pilot reps; and 3) optional one on one interviews for 3 to 4 reps who have strong opinions. We will consolidate all of that into A5 for T7. This should give us enough depth without being too heavy.

That feedback structure sounds balanced. We just need to make sure the weekly survey is easy to access and that managers remind reps to fill it in. I can help set up the survey template and schedule the final group call as part of T6.

From the sales side, the proposed cadence is acceptable. If we keep the survey to 3 quick questions and schedule the final call at a predictable time, managers will support participation. I will brief the mid-market manager on this plan so there are no surprises.

I am fine with the 4 week duration and the feedback approach. For success thresholds, do we want to define minimum targets for opportunity creation uplift and adoption rate during the pilot For example, at least a 20 percent increase in cross-sell opportunity creation in the pilot teams versus their baseline, and at least 70 percent of eligible opportunities tagged as cross-sell.

Setting thresholds will help. I suggest we aim for: 1) at least 20 percent uplift in cross-sell opportunity creation versus the same teams baseline, 2) at least 10 percent uplift in win rate on cross-sell opportunities, and 3) at least 70 percent of eligible opportunities correctly tagged and following the checklist. We will track these in A3 for the pilot cohort and summarize results in A5.

Those thresholds are ambitious but realistic for a focused pilot. I support using them as our success criteria. If we fall short on one metric but see strong qualitative feedback, we can still decide how to adjust before full rollout.

To recap the pilot plan for T6 and T7: 1) duration is 4 weeks; 2) participants are 6 mid-market reps, 4 high-growth SMB reps, plus 2 enterprise reps using the renewal path from A2; 3) scope is mid-market and high-growth SMB segments as defined in A1, with enterprise as an additional input; 4) success metrics are uplift in cross-sell opportunity creation and win rate, plus adoption rate based on CRM tagging and checklist usage as defined in A3; and 5) feedback will be collected via weekly pulse surveys, a final group call, and a few one on one interviews, consolidated into A5. Unless there are objections, I will treat this as our agreed pilot scope, participating teams, and success criteria.
This summary matches my understanding. I am aligned with the teams, duration, and metrics. From the sales side, we are ready to move forward with this pilot setup.
Aligned as well. The thresholds and feedback plan are clear, and the selected teams are a good fit for testing the playbook.
Given the confirmations, we can lock the pilot scope and metrics. I will coordinate with the managers to confirm the final list of reps and calendar the start date so we can kick off next week.

threads.thread_goal: Lock training approach, rollout checklist, and launch communication.

messages.text: Moving to training and launch. Based on the pilot design and A2, I drafted a training and rollout checklist in A6 and a first version of the launch communication pack in A7, covering T8, T10, and T11. Proposal: 1) a 60 minute virtual training per region, combining overview of A2, live demo in the CRM, and role plays; 2) A6 as the checklist for managers to confirm readiness; 3) A7 as the email and meeting templates for Q3 launch; and 4) governance reminders aligned with A4. Please review A6 and A7 and share any concerns on format, timing, or messaging before we lock the plan.

On A6, the checklist is comprehensive, but I am slightly worried that a 60 minute session might be hard to schedule for all regions before Q3 starts, given other initiatives. Could we consider a 45 minute core session plus optional 30 minute follow up clinics for those who want more practice That might increase attendance while still giving enough depth.

Looking at A7, the messaging is clear on benefits, but I would suggest we add one concrete example per segment, using the pairings from A1. That will help reps immediately see how the playbook applies to their accounts. Also, in the manager talking points, can we highlight that targets will be set in coordination with finance as part of T9, so it does not feel like an extra quota on top of everything else.

In A6, there is a step about confirming that discount and approval rules are understood. I am not sure if we should cover all of A4 in the training or just the parts specific to cross-sell. Covering everything might be too much for one session.

On timing, if we go with a 45 minute core session plus optional clinics as @231 suggested, we should still make sure every rep attends at least one live session before using the playbook. Maybe A6 can include a simple attendance tracker for managers to confirm completion before Q3 launch.

I like the 45 minute core plus optional 30 minute clinic approach. We can structure the core session around why we are doing this, walk through A2, and show the CRM steps, then use the clinics for deeper role plays. I will update A6 and T8 to reflect this format.

Good call on concrete examples. I will add one short scenario per segment in A7, using the approved pairings from A1, and I will adjust the manager talking points to emphasize that cross-sell targets will be set with finance as part of T9, not as an extra quota layer. That should help with positioning.

On A4, I agree we should not try to cover everything. In the training, we will focus on the parts that are specific to cross-sell, mainly the approval thresholds for add on products and the exceptions process. I will adjust A6 so the checklist item is about confirming that reps know where to find A4 and understand the cross-sell specific rules, rather than reviewing the entire policy in the session.

I can add an attendance tracker section to A6 with columns for rep name, session date, and completion status. Managers can use that to confirm that all reps in their team have attended either the core session or a clinic before they start using the playbook.

For the examples in A7, I suggest we keep them very short, one or two sentences each, so the email does not become too long. We can always provide more detailed scenarios in the training deck. I can help draft the mid-market example based on a recent deal.

On scheduling, do we already have a target week for the core sessions If Q3 starts in three weeks, we probably need to run the core sessions in week minus 2 and the clinics in week minus 1, so that everyone is ready by launch. It might be useful to reflect that timeline in A6 and T8.

Yes, timeline wise I propose: core sessions in the week two weeks before Q3 start, clinics in the week right before Q3, and launch communications from A7 going out two days before Q3. I will update A6 and T8 with this schedule so it is clear for managers.

I rechecked A6 after your edits and the reference to A4 is now more focused. The checklist item about cross-sell specific rules is clear enough for managers to confirm understanding without turning the training into a policy session.

With the updated format and timeline, A6 now reads as a practical rollout plan. We have training, governance reminders, CRM readiness, and communication steps all in one place. From a project side, I am comfortable using this as the baseline for all regions.

On A7, after your updates, the key messages are clear: why we are doing this, what changes for reps, and what support they will get. The segment examples help make it concrete. I do not see any major gaps from the sales communication perspective.

Agreed. The only small suggestion is to add a line in the manager script encouraging teams to bring one live opportunity to the training so they can immediately apply the playbook. That tends to increase engagement.
Good idea. I will add a short prompt in the manager talking points in A7 asking reps to come with one live opportunity to work on during the session. With that, I think A7 is ready to go.

To summarize the plan: 1) training format is a 45 minute core virtual session per region plus optional 30 minute clinics, with attendance tracked in A6; 2) A6 now includes the rollout checklist, attendance tracker, governance reminders linked to A4, and the timeline aligned with Q3 start; 3) A7 contains the launch emails and manager scripts with segment specific examples from A1, clear positioning on targets being set with finance via T9, and a prompt for reps to bring a live opportunity; and 4) launch communications will go out two days before Q3. Unless there are objections, I will treat this as our final training format, rollout timeline, and launch communication pack.
This summary matches what we need. From the sales side, I am aligned with the training format and the communication content and timing.
Aligned as well. The plan feels realistic for the teams and should give us a solid start for Q3.
Great, thanks all. I will proceed with finalizing A6 and A7 and coordinating with regional managers to schedule the sessions and send the launch communications as planned.

threads.thread_goal: Review early Q3 results and agree on improvement actions.

messages.text: We now have the first 4 weeks of Q3 data and a draft of the performance and lessons learned report in A8 for T12. Using the KPIs from A3, early results show: 1) cross-sell opportunity creation up 18 percent overall versus baseline, with stronger uplift in mid-market than SMB; 2) cross-sell win rate up 7 percent; and 3) adoption, measured by correct tagging and checklist usage, at around 65 percent of eligible opportunities. A8 also summarizes qualitative feedback from A5. We need to agree on which improvement actions to prioritize for the next iteration of the playbook and rollout. Please review A8 and share your top two or three actions you think we should focus on.

Looking at A8, the main gap I see is adoption, especially in SMB. Many reps mention that the playbook is clear but they sometimes skip the checklist when they are in a hurry. My top two actions would be: 1) simplify the SMB checklist in A2 and A6 to focus on the two or three most critical items; and 2) work with managers to include a short cross-sell review in their weekly pipeline meetings, using the dashboard views from A3 to reinforce usage.

I agree adoption is the main lever. From the field feedback in A5 and A8, another theme is that some reps are unsure which pairing to lead with in SMB when time is short. I would prioritize: 1) adding a simple default pairing recommendation per segment in A2 and A7, so reps know what to propose if they have only a few minutes; and 2) creating a short refresher micro session or video that managers can use in team huddles, rather than relying only on the original training.

In A8, there are a few comments about confusion on discount approvals for bundled cross-sell offers. Even though A4 is referenced, some reps still ask their managers for clarification. Maybe we should tighten the guidance in A4 and A2 with one or two concrete examples of typical cross-sell discounts, so reps feel more confident without escalating every time.

From a data perspective, A8 shows that mid-market is performing close to our pilot thresholds, but SMB is lagging both in opportunity creation and adoption. I would suggest we focus our next iteration on SMB first, rather than changing everything at once. That means prioritizing improvements to the SMB path in A2, the checklist in A6, and the examples in A7, while keeping the mid-market flow mostly stable.

Simplifying the SMB checklist and reinforcing usage in pipeline reviews makes sense. We can reduce the checklist to the two or three must have items and add a standard cross-sell review section to the manager pipeline template, using the A3 dashboard views. That should help drive adoption without adding separate meetings.

On default pairings, we already have the top three per segment in A1, but we can highlight a primary default per segment in A2 and A7 for quick conversations. For SMB, that would likely be starter package plus onboarding support, unless we see data in A8 suggesting another pairing performs better. I will double check the numbers before we lock that.

Data in A8 suggests that starter plus onboarding support has slightly higher conversion than starter plus analytics light in SMB, so using it as the default makes sense. We can still keep the other pairings as alternatives in A2 for more tailored situations.

For the refresher, maybe we can record a 10 minute walkthrough of the SMB path in A2, including one example conversation, and link it from A6 and A7. Managers could play it in team huddles without needing a full new training session.

On the discount examples, I can draft two or three typical cross-sell scenarios with the corresponding approval paths based on A4 and share them for review. We can then add them as an appendix to A4 and reference them in A2 so reps have something concrete to follow.

If we add the 10 minute SMB walkthrough, we should also track its usage, at least roughly. Maybe we can ask managers to confirm in A6 whether they have played it in their team huddles, so we know which teams have received the refresher.

Given the data and feedback, I agree we should focus this iteration on SMB. Combining the points raised, a draft list of improvement actions could be: 1) simplify the SMB checklist in A2 and A6 to two or three critical items; 2) define and highlight a default SMB pairing in A2 and A7, based on A8 data; 3) create a 10 minute SMB refresher walkthrough and link it in A6 and A7; 4) add cross-sell review to weekly pipeline meetings using A3 views; and 5) add two or three concrete discount examples to A4 and reference them in A2. Let us confirm if these are the right priorities or if anything should be swapped out.

This list reflects the main pain points I hear from managers. If we had to prioritize within it, I would put checklist simplification and default pairing first, then the refresher content and pipeline review, and finally the discount examples. The last one is important but affects fewer deals than the basic adoption issues.

I am aligned with that prioritization. If we can implement the first four actions quickly, we should see a noticeable impact on SMB adoption. The discount examples can follow shortly after without blocking the rest.
I agree with the list and the order. I can start working on the discount examples in parallel, but I do not think they need to delay the other changes.

From a project planning view, the first four actions are relatively light changes to A2, A6, A7, and manager routines, so we can implement them within the next two weeks. The A4 examples might need a quick check with finance, but as @447210 said, they can run in parallel.

Thanks for the input. To close this out, I propose we formally prioritize the following improvement actions for the next iteration: 1) simplify the SMB checklist in A2 and A6 to focus on the most critical items; 2) define and highlight a default SMB pairing in A2 and A7, based on the performance data in A8; 3) create and distribute a 10 minute SMB refresher walkthrough, linked in A6 and A7, and track its use via the checklist; 4) embed a short cross-sell review in weekly pipeline meetings using the A3 dashboard views; and 5) add two or three concrete cross-sell discount examples to A4 and reference them in A2, validating with finance as needed. Unless there are objections, we will treat these as the prioritized improvement actions for this cycle.
Aligned with this set of actions and the focus on SMB. I will brief the relevant managers so they are ready to support the checklist changes and the new pipeline review step.
No objections from my side. These priorities make sense and are feasible within the next couple of weeks.
Great, we will proceed with this improvement set and update A2, A6, A7, A3, and A4 accordingly, then refresh A8 once we have another cycle of data.
